en: The *Sifen Sengjieben* (The Four-Part Monastic Code) translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kaśmīra during the Later Qin Dynasty, as transmitted by the Dharmaguptaka school.
I prostrate and pay homage to all Buddhas, And to the Dharma and the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus.
Now I shall expound the Vinaya Dharma, so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time.
The precepts are like the ocean, boundless; like jewels, one never tires of seeking them.
Those who wish to protect the noble wealth of the Dharma, assemble and listen as I speak.
To eliminate the four *pārājika* rules, And to extinguish the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules,
As well as the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses— Gathered assembly,
listen as I speak! Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, [Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa].
Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni—these World-Honored Ones of great virtue have explained this matter for me.
Now I wish to explain it well; may all you worthy ones listen together.
Just as a person whose feet are injured is unable to travel anywhere, so it is with one who has violated the precepts:
they cannot be reborn among gods or humans.
If one wishes to be born in the heavens, or to be born in the human realm, [one must guard the precepts].
One should always protect the feet of the precepts, never allowing them to be damaged.
Just as a driver entering a perilous path suffers the anxiety of losing a pin or breaking an axle, so it is with the violation of the precepts;
at the time of death, one harbors fear.
As when a person looks into a mirror, Joy or sorrow arises according to whether they are handsome or ugly;
So it is with the recitation of the precepts: Grief or joy arises according to whether one is complete or ruined.
As when two armies engage in battle, The brave advance while the timid retreat.
The recitation of the precepts is likewise thus: from purity comes peace, and from defilement arises fear.
Among those in the world, the king is supreme; among all flowing waters, the ocean is supreme;
among all the stars, the moon is supreme; and among all holy ones, the Buddha is supreme.
Among all the various codes of discipline, the Sūtra of Precepts is supreme;
the Tathāgata established these prohibitions and recites them every half-month.
"Is the Saṃgha assembled in harmony?"
Has anyone who has not received the full ordination departed?
Have any bhikṣus who did not come declared their *chanda* and purity?
Who sent the bhikṣuṇī to receive the instruction?
"What shall the Saṃgha do now that it is in harmony?
He replied, "We shall perform the *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the precepts."
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Today is the fifteenth day for the Saṃgha’s poṣadha and the recitation of the precepts.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen, so that we may recite the precepts in harmony."
The announcement is thus made. Venerable sirs!
I now wish to recite the precepts; as the assembly is gathered before me, listen in silence and reflect upon them well.
If there are those who have committed an offense, they should confess it; those who have not committed an offense should remain silent.
By remaining silent, it should be known that the Saṃgha is pure.
If anyone should raise an accusation against another, they should immediately answer according to the facts.
Thus, when these bhikṣus are among the assembly, they shall be reminded up to three times; if they remember having committed an offense, they must confess it.
One who does not confess commits the offense of intentional lying.
The Buddha has taught that intentional lying is a dharma that obstructs the Path. Therefore, if a bhikṣu remembers and knows he has committed an offense and desires purity, he must confess it.
Confessing brings peace and security;
failing to confess causes the offense to deepen further.
Venerable sirs!
I have already recited the introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
Now I ask the Venerable Ones:
Are you pure in this regard?
Thus, O Venerable Ones, a second and a third time it is asked:
"In this matter you are pure, for you remain silent; thus I shall hold it to be so.
"O Venerable Ones!"
These four *pārājika* dharmas are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.

If a bhikṣu, who shares the same precepts and the same training as other bhikṣus, does not renounce the precepts and does not repent for his weakness in morality, yet commits an act of impurity by engaging in sexual intercourse—
even with an animal— [he is defeated].
This bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and shall not dwell in community with us.
"If a bhikṣu, whether in a village or in a secluded place, takes what is not given with a thieving mind;

according to the law regarding taking what is not given, if he is seized by a king or a king’s minister, or is executed, bound, or driven out of the country: [he is one who has committed a pārājika offense and shall not dwell in community with us]."
"You are a thief!
You are deluded! You have no knowledge!"
“A bhikṣu who steals in this manner commits a pārājika offense; he is not to live in community.
If a bhikṣu intentionally takes the life of a human being with his own hand, provides a person with a knife, praises death, or enthusiastically encourages death, saying:
‘Ho! [Why do you live?]’”
"Man, what is the use of this wretched life?
It is better to die than to live.
Thinking thus, he considers various means, praising death and encouraging it with delight.
This bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and shall not dwell in communion.
"If a bhikṣu, while having no actual realization, claims for himself:
'I have attained the state of a superior person; I have entered the sublime Dharma of noble wisdom; I know this; I see this.'"
At a later time, whether questioned or not, desiring to purify himself, he speaks thus:
"I truly did not know or see, yet I said that I knew and saw; this was a false, deceptive, and lying speech."
"Excepting one who has overweening pride,
this bhikṣu is defeated (pārājika) and shall not dwell in communion.
Venerable sirs!"
I have already explained the four *pārājika* rules.
If a bhikṣu commits any one of these *pārājika* rules, he may not dwell together with the bhikṣus as before, nor may he do so hereafter.
This bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and should not live in community with us.
Now I ask the venerable ones:
Are you pure in this matter?
Thus it was said three times: "Venerable sirs!
Since you are silent, you are pure in this matter; thus shall this be held.
"Venerable sirs!"
These thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra.
If a bhikṣu intentionally emits semen by manipulating his own organ, except during a dream, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind, makes physical contact with a woman—whether by grasping her hand, grasping her hair, or touching any part of her body—it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
"If a bhikṣu, with lustful intent, addresses a woman with lewd and coarse language regarding sexual desire, for whatever such lewd and coarse language he utters, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
"If a bhikṣu, with lustful intent, in the presence of a woman, praises his own person, saying:

'Sister! I practice the holy life, I am observant of the precepts and diligent, and I cultivate wholesome dharmas; you may offer this dharma of sexual desire to me, for such an offering is the foremost and most excellent.'"
One who speaks in such a manner commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

If a bhikṣu acts as a go-between for mutual liaisons, conveying a man’s intent to a woman and a woman’s intent to a man—whether for the purpose of formal marriage or for illicit intercourse, even for a mere moment—he commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
"If a bhikṣu should beg for materials to build a house that has no owner and is for his own use, he must build it according to the prescribed measurements.
Regarding these measurements: the length shall be twelve spans of the Buddha’s hands, and the internal width seven spans."
One should take other bhikṣus to inspect the site; those bhikṣus shall indicate whether it is a place free from difficulties and free from obstructions.

If a bhikṣu, for himself and without an owner, begs materials to build a hut on a site that has difficulties or obstructions, and does not take other bhikṣus to inspect the site, or if he builds it in excess of the prescribed measure, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

"If a bhikṣu wishes to build a large dwelling for himself that has an owner, he should take other bhikṣus to inspect the site; those bhikṣus should inspect the site to ensure it is free from difficulties and free from obstructions."
If a bhikṣu, in a dangerous or obstructed location, has a large dwelling built for himself that has a patron, and does not take other bhikṣus along to inspect the site, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
"If a bhikṣu, being overcome by ill will, should defame a bhikṣu who is not guilty of a pārājika offense with a groundless pārājika charge, desiring to ruin that bhikṣu’s pure conduct."
At another time, whether questioned or not, if he knows that this matter was spoken without basis and says,
"I spoke these words out of anger," if a bhikṣu speaks thus, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

"If a bhikṣu, being overcome by ill will, takes up a mere fragment from a matter of a different category and, though the bhikṣu is not one who has committed a pārājika offense, slanders him with a groundless pārājika charge, desiring to ruin that bhikṣu’s pure conduct."
If, at a later time, whether questioned or unasked, he knows that this was taken from a portion of a different matter,
and that monk says of himself, "I spoke these words out of anger," it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

"If a bhikṣu seeks to cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha, employing means to adopt the practices that cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha, and persistently maintains them without relinquishing them,
other bhikṣus should admonish that bhikṣu, saying:
'Venerable sir!'"
Do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha; do not employ means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; do not accept the teachings that lead to a schism, nor persistently maintain them without relinquishing them.
Venerable One!

You should be in harmony with the Saṃgha, rejoicing without contention, studying under the same teacher as one body, like water and milk blending together, so that within the Buddha-dharma there may be increase and a dwelling in peace and happiness.
When that bhikṣu thus admonishes him, if he persists and does not relinquish [his position],
those bhikṣus should admonish him three times so that he may relinquish this matter, even unto the third admonition.
"If he relinquishes it, that is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If a bhikṣu has other factions—whether one, two, three, or even countless [supporters]..."
That bhikṣu says to those bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!

Do not admonish this bhikṣu; this bhikṣu is a speaker of the Dharma, a speaker of the Vinaya. What this bhikṣu speaks, we find pleasing in our hearts; what this bhikṣu speaks, we accept with our minds."
That bhikṣu should admonish this bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir, do not speak thus, saying:
'This bhikṣu is a speaker of Dharma, a speaker of Vinaya; what this bhikṣu says, we find pleasing in our hearts; what this bhikṣu says, we approve in our hearts.'"
Why is this? Because, Venerable Sir,
this bhikṣu is not a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Dharma, nor is he a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Vinaya.
Do not seek to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; you should instead desire harmony with the Saṃgha.
Venerable sirs!

Be in harmony with the Saṃgha, rejoicing and free from dispute, studying under the same teacher as one body, like water and milk blending together; thus, within the Buddha-dharma, there will be increase and a dwelling in peace and happiness.
When that bhikṣu thus admonishes him and he persists in his refusal to relinquish it,
those bhikṣus should admonish him three times so that he may relinquish this matter, up to and including the third admonition.
"If he relinquishes it, it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
'If a bhikṣu, residing in a village or a town, engages in evil conduct and defiles families..."
They have been seen and heard to engage in evil conduct;
they have been seen and heard to defile the families of others.
The bhikṣus say to this bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!
You have committed evil deeds and defiled families.
Your evil conduct has been both seen and heard."
"You have defiled the families of others; this is both seen and heard.
Venerable sir!
You have practiced evil conduct and defiled the families of others. You should now depart from this village; you need not remain here."
That bhikṣu said to those bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!

Among the bhikṣus there are those who have affection, those who have hatred, those who have fear, and those who have delusion; thus, among bhikṣus who have committed the same offense, some are expelled while others are not."
The bhikṣus replied,
"Venerable sir!
Do not speak such words!"
He said:
"The bhikṣus possess attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion; thus, among bhikṣus who have committed the same offense, some are expelled while others are not."
"For what reason? Because, Venerable Sir,
the bhikṣus are without attachment, without aversion, without fear, and without delusion."
"You have committed evil conduct and defiled families.
Your evil conduct has been both seen and heard;
your defiling of families has also been both seen and heard."
When that bhikṣu thus admonishes him and he persists in his refusal to relinquish it,
those bhikṣus should admonish him up to three times so that he may relinquish this matter— even unto the third admonition.
"If he abandons it, it is well;
if he does not abandon it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If a bhikṣu is of an evil nature and does not accept the words of admonition, and when the bhikṣus have admonished him according to the Dharma regarding the rules of training, he himself does not accept the words of admonition and says:"
"Venerable sirs!
Do not speak to me of what is good or bad, nor shall I speak to you venerable sirs of what is good or bad.
Venerable sirs, please desist!"
"Do not admonish me.
Then that bhikṣu said to this bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!..."
Do not refuse to accept admonition yourself; Venerable One, you should accept admonition yourself.
Just as the Venerable One admonishes the bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma, so too shall the bhikṣus admonish the Venerable One in accordance with the Dharma.
"In this way, the community of the Buddha's disciples shall attain increase, admonishing one another, instructing one another,
and confessing their faults to one another. When that bhikṣu thus receives such admonition, if he persists and does not relinquish his position,
those bhikṣus should admonish him three times so that he may relinquish that matter, continuing up to the third admonition.
"If he relinquishes it, that is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Venerable sirs!"
I have already explained the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas: nine are offenses upon the first commission, and four require up to three admonitions.
If a bhikṣu commits any one of these dharmas and knowingly conceals it, the Saṃgha shall compel him to undergo *parivāsa*;
once he has completed the *parivāsa*, the Saṃgha shall grant him six nights of *mānatva*.
Once the *mānatva* penance has been performed, there remains the matter of the removal of the offense (*āpattivyutthāna*).

This bhikṣu’s offense must be removed before an assembly of twenty monks. If even one person is missing and the assembly of twenty is not complete when the bhikṣu’s offense is removed, that bhikṣu’s offense cannot be cleared; furthermore, the other bhikṣus may censure him. This is the proper occasion.
Now I ask the venerable ones:
Are you pure in this matter?
Thus it is asked three times: "Venerable ones!"
"In this matter, we are pure, because of our silence; thus shall this matter be upheld.
"Venerable sirs!
These two indeterminate rules (aniyata-dharma) are recited in the Pratimokṣa Sūtra every half-month."
If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded, concealed place, a suitable location for sexual intercourse, and speaks improper words,
and there is a faithful upāsikā who accuses him of one of three offenses—
whether a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a pāyattika;
If a monk sitting in this assembly says of himself,
"I have committed this offense," he should be dealt with according to each of the three rules:

Whether it be a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika*, one should deal with that bhikṣu according to the law as stated by a laywoman (*upāsikā*) of established faith; this is called an indeterminate rule (*aniyata-dharma*).
"If a bhikṣu sits with a woman in an uncovered place, in a spot where sexual intercourse cannot be committed, and utters coarse and wicked words, speaking of matters of sexual desire."
There was a female lay follower established in faith who, regarding each of two categories of offenses—
either a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*— spoke thus;
the bhikṣu sitting there then spoke for himself:
"I have committed this offense.

Regarding these two categories of offenses, he should be dealt with according to each one—whether it be a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*—just as the laywoman who has faith has described. One should deal with that bhikṣu according to the Dharma; this is called an *aniyata-dharma*.
"Venerable sirs!
I have already recited the two *aniyata* dharmas.
Now I ask the venerable sirs: [Is it pure in this matter?]"
"Is there purity herein?
Thus he asks three times: "Venerable sirs!
Since there is silence, you are pure herein. This matter is thus maintained."
"Venerable sirs!
These thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas are recited in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* every half-month."
If a bhikṣu, having finished his robes and having had the kaṭhina cloth withdrawn, keeps an extra robe for ten days, he may retain it provided it has not been formally assigned as a gift;
if he exceeds this period, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

"If a bhikṣu, having finished making his robes and having had the kaṭhina privileges withdrawn, should stay overnight apart from any one of his three robes at a different location for even a single night—unless by formal authorization of the Saṃgha (saṃghakamma)—it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika)."

"If a bhikṣu, having finished his robes and having had the kaṭhina privileges withdrawn, should obtain an out-of-season robe and desire it, he may accept it; having accepted it, he must quickly have it made into a robe."
If it is sufficient, that is well;
if it is insufficient, one may keep it for up to one month in order to fulfill the requirement.
If one exceeds this period, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"If a bhikṣu receives a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange for another item, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu causes a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to wash an old robe, or to dye it, or to beat it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."

“If a bhikṣu asks for a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, except at the appropriate time, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika).”
The exceptions are: when a bhikṣu’s robes have been stolen, lost, burned, or carried away by water; this is the proper occasion.

"If a bhikṣu’s robes have been stolen, lost, burned, or carried away by water, and a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative invites him and offers many robes, that bhikṣu should receive the robes with moderation."
If one accepts more than this, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a monk, for whom a householder or a householder’s wife has prepared the price for robes, saying:
'Take this price for robes and give it to such-and-such a monk.'"
"Suppose this bhikṣu, without having previously received an invitation for a formal robe-offering, goes to a householder's home and speaks thus:
'Excellent, householder!
Prepare such a price for a robe and give it to me.'"
If, for the sake of desiring something fine, he should obtain a robe [with that money], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If two laymen or two laywomen provide the price for such a robe for a bhikṣu, saying:
'We have provided this price for a robe to give to such-and-such a bhikṣu.'"
"Suppose this bhikṣu, having not previously received an invitation for a formal robe-offering, goes to the houses of two lay devotees and speaks thus:
'Excellent, lay devotees!
Prepare such robes as these and give them to me; let us together make one robe.'"
If, for the sake of desiring something fine, he should obtain it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a monk, by a king, a royal minister, a brahmin, a householder, or a householder’s wife, has a messenger sent to deliver the price of a robe with the instruction:
'Take this price for a robe and give it to such-and-such a monk. "
That messenger went to where the bhikṣu was and said to him:
"Venerable sir!
These robe-funds have been sent for your sake; please accept them."
The bhikṣu should speak thus to that messenger:
"I should not now accept this price for robes; if I require robes, I shall accept them when it is the proper time and they are pure."
The messenger said to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir,
are there any attendants?"
The bhikṣu who needs robes should say:
"There is! Whether it be a monastery attendant or an upāsaka, this person is a steward for the bhikṣus and constantly performs services for them."
The messenger went to the person in charge, gave him the price for the robe, and returned to where the bhikṣu was, saying:
"Venerable sir!
I have already given the price for the robe to the person in charge whom you indicated."
"Venerable sir!
Know that the time has come; go there and you shall obtain robes.
The bhikṣu who requires robes should then go to the person in charge of affairs and speak these words two or three times:
"I need a robe.
If he succeeds in obtaining a robe after being reminded a second or third time, that is well.
If he does not obtain a robe, he should stand silently before him for a fourth, fifth, or sixth time, thereby causing him to remember.
If he stands silently before [the donor] four, five, or six times, and if he obtains the robe, it is well.
If he does not obtain the robe, and he seeks to obtain it beyond that number of times, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If he does not obtain the robe, he should either go there himself or send a messenger to the place from which it originated and say:
"Previously, you sent a messenger with the price for a robe to a certain bhikṣu; however, that bhikṣu did not ultimately receive the robe."
"Go back and take it; do not let it be lost. This is the proper time.
[The Ten Matters: "If a bhikṣu makes a bedding out of mixed wild silk-cotton, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
“If a bhikṣu makes a bedding out of new, pure black sheep’s wool, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika).
If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding, he should use two parts of pure black sheep’s wool, three parts of white, and four parts of variegated wool.”

If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding mat without using two parts of pure black wool, three parts of white, and four parts of variegated wool, he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika).
"If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding or mat, he should use it for six years.
If, before the six years have elapsed, he does not relinquish the old one and makes another new one—unless by formal authorization of the Saṃgha—he commits an offense of *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat, he must take a piece from an old one, measuring one span in length and breadth, and patch it onto the new one for the purpose of discoloring it."

If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat and does not take a piece of old material, even as small as one span in length and breadth, and paste it onto the new material to spoil its color, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣu obtains wool while traveling on a journey, and the bhikṣu requires it, he may take it.
If there is no one to carry it, he may carry it himself for a distance of three yojanas."
If one carries it oneself when there is no one else to carry it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu causes a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to wash, dye, or card wool, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu takes gold, silver, or coin with his own hand, or instructs another to take them, or accepts them by word of mouth, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
“If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling gold, silver, or precious objects, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika).
“If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of trade and commerce, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.”
Twenty Matters: "If a bhikṣu keeps an extra alms-bowl without having made it a formal gift (apariśuddha-dāna), he may do so for up to ten days.
If he exceeds this period, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika)."
"If a bhikṣu, whose bowl is broken but has fewer than five patches and is not leaking, seeks a new bowl for the sake of its beauty,
and obtains one, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense."
That bhikṣu should go before the Saṃgha to relinquish it; the most inferior bowl among them should be taken in turn and given to him to keep until it breaks.
"If a bhikṣu himself begs for thread and has a weaver who is not a relative weave it into a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."

"If a bhikṣu, when a householder or a householder’s wife has commissioned a weaver to weave a robe for that bhikṣu, goes to the weaver’s place before having been invited by them and says to the weaver:
'Weave this robe for me; weave it very well, making it wide, long, firm, fine, and perfectly even; I will give you a small amount of payment.'"
"If a bhikṣu gives a price, even the value of a single meal, and obtains a robe [in exchange], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu has previously given a robe to another bhikṣu, and later, out of anger, either seizes it himself or causes another to seize it, saying:
'Give me back my robe; I will not give it to you.'"
That bhikṣu should return the robe;
if he takes it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, being ill, keeps ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, or rock honey, he may consume them for a period of seven days."
If one exceeds this limit, it is an offense of forfeiture and expiation (niḥsargika-pāyattika).
"If a bhikṣu has one month remaining of the spring season, he should seek a rain-bath robe and use it for bathing during the [subsequent] half-month."
If a bhikṣu seeks a rain-bath robe one month before the spring season begins, or uses it for bathing half a month before that time, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu has less than ten days remaining until the end of the three-month summer retreat, and there is an urgent gift of robes, he should accept it."
Once received, it may be kept until the time for [receiving] robes.
If one keeps it beyond that period, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣu, having completed the three-month summer retreat and reached the full fifteenth day of the eighth month, should reside in a remote place characterized by doubt, fear, or danger, he may leave any one of his three robes within a village dwelling; furthermore, due to a valid cause, he may be separated from his robe while staying overnight for up to six nights."
If one exceeds [the limit], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another intends to give property to the Saṃgha, diverts it for himself, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
The Thirty Matters: "Venerable sirs!
I have already recited the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas.
Now I ask the venerable sirs: [Are you pure in this matter?]"
"Is there purity herein?
Thus he asks three times: "Venerable sirs!
Since you are silent, you are pure herein; this matter shall be held as such."
"Venerable sirs!
These ninety *pāyattika* rules are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra:
'If a bhikṣu intentionally utters a falsehood, it is a *pāyattika* offense.'"
"If a bhikṣu disparages another bhikṣu by way of his lineage, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu speaks with double-tongued speech, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu sleeps in the same room as a woman, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu sleeps together with one who has not received the full ordination, and stays beyond two nights until dawn on the third night, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu recites the scriptures together with a person who has not yet received full ordination, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense, speaks of it to a person who has not received full ordination—except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha—it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu speaks of a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma) to a person who has not received full ordination, saying:
'I know this; I have seen this,' and he speaks truthfully of what he knows and sees, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu teaches the Dharma to a woman for more than five or six sentences, it is a pāyattika,
except when a man capable of understanding is present.
"If a bhikṣu digs the earth with his own hands or instructs another to dig it, it is a pāyattika."
10. "If a bhikṣu destroys a village of spirits, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu speaks falsely and maliciously to annoy another, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu reviles [another] out of resentment, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu takes a monastic rope bed, wooden bed, bedding, or sitting mat, spreads it himself on an open space, or instructs another to spread it;
and then departs without putting it away himself or instructing another to put it away, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, within a monastic dwelling, spreads bedding or cushions belonging to the Saṃgha—whether spreading them himself or instructing another to spread them—and sits or lies upon them;
if he then departs from that place without putting them away himself or instructing another to put them away, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, knowing in advance that another bhikṣu already occupies a dwelling, later comes and forcibly spreads out bedding and stays there, thinking:
'If he finds it cramped, he will surely avoid me and leave.'"
"By acting as a cause for this, and not through any other posture, it is a *pāyattika*.

'If a bhikṣu, out of anger toward another bhikṣu and being displeased with him, within a communal dwelling (*saṃghārāma*), either personally drags him out or instructs another to drag him out, it is a *pāyattika*.'"
"If a bhikṣu, on an upper story of a multi-storied building, sits or lies down upon a rope bed or a wooden bed with detachable legs, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that water contains living creatures, uses it himself to sprinkle mud or grass, or instructs another to do so, it is a pāyattika."

"If a bhikṣu wishes to construct a large dwelling, regarding the doors, windows, lattices, and various decorative fittings, he may direct the covering with thatch for up to two or three layers; if he exceeds this, it is a pāyattika."
20. “If a bhikṣu, not having been appointed by the Saṃgha, teaches the bhikṣuṇīs, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu, though appointed by the Saṃgha, teaches the bhikṣuṇīs until sunset, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣu says to other bhikṣus:
'The bhikṣus teach the bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of food and drink,' it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange for another, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place with a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu makes an appointment to travel together with a bhikṣuṇī along the same path, even as far as a village, except at other times, it is a pāyattika."
"Other times" refers to when traveling with a companion through a place where there is apprehension or fear;
this is the [permissible] time. "If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to ride in a boat, whether going upriver or downriver—except for crossing directly across—it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that food was obtained through the mediation of a bhikṣuṇī’s praise, eats it, except when the donor had a prior intention, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a woman to travel along the same path, even as far as a village, it is a pāyattika."
30. "If a monk, at a place where a single meal is offered, being free from illness, should accept more than one meal, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
"If a monk eats by taking turns [at different houses], except during the remaining times, it is a *pāyattika* offense."
"Except at other times"—the time of illness and the time of receiving robes; these are the [permitted] times.
"If a bhikṣu eats separately from the community, except at other times, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika)."

The exceptions are: when one is ill, when robes are being given, when robes are being made, when traveling on a journey, when traveling by boat, during a great assembly, or when śramaṇas are distributing food—these are the appropriate times.

"If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a donor and is earnestly invited to receive cakes, parched grain, or cooked rice, and the bhikṣu requires them, he should accept two or three bowls. Having brought them to the monastery, he should divide them and give them to the other bhikṣus to eat."
If a bhikṣu who is not ill receives more than two or three bowls of food and, having brought it to the monastery, does not share it with other bhikṣus for them to eat, it is a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣu, having finished his meal, should at another time accept an invitation and eat further food without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual for leftover food), it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu knows that another bhikṣu has finished his meal, yet, having accepted an invitation, persistently invites him to eat without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta*, saying:
'Venerable sir!'"
"Take this food.
For this reason, and no other—if one intends to cause another to commit an offense, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu eats at an improper time, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu eats food that has been stored overnight, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu eats food not offered to him, or places medicine into his mouth—except for water and tooth-sticks—it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, being free from illness, seeks for himself fine foods such as milk, curd, fish, or meat, it is a pāyattika."
40. “If a bhikṣu gives food with his own hand to a male follower of another sect or a female follower of another sect, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣu, having already accepted an invitation, goes to another household before or after the meal without informing another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.”
Except at other times, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Other times" refers to the time of illness, the time of making robes, and the time of receiving robes; these are the [permissible] times.
"If a bhikṣu, when there is treasure in a family home, sits down forcefully, it is a *pāyattika*."
“If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place with a woman in a household where there is treasure, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in an open space, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣu says to other bhikṣus:
'Venerable sirs, come together to the village; I shall give you food.'"
That bhikṣu, even when they had reached the village, did not instruct anyone to give food to this bhikṣu, but said:
"Go away! I do not find pleasure in sitting or speaking with you; I find pleasure in sitting and speaking alone."
For this reason, and no other, if one sends [a person] away through expedient means, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a monk is invited to receive medicine for four months, a monk who is not ill should accept it."
If one accepts [an invitation] beyond the limit—except for a regular invitation, a repeated invitation, a partial invitation, or a lifelong invitation—it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu goes to view an army formation, except when there is a specific reason, it is a *pāyattika*."
“If a bhikṣu has a reason to go among an army and stays for more than two nights, reaching a third night, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣu stays among an army for two or three nights and at any time observes military formations and combat, or observes the power of a marching army, elephants, or horses, it is a pāyattika.”
50. "If a bhikṣu drinks alcohol, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu plays in water, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu tickles another bhikṣu with his fingers, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu does not accept admonition, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu terrifies another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣu bathes once every half-month, it is permissible for a bhikṣu who is not ill to do so.
If he bathes more frequently than that, except during other times, it is a pāyattika offense.

‘Other times’ refers to the heat of summer, the time of illness, the time of manual labor, the time of wind, the time of rain, and when one has traveled a long distance—these are the [permissible] times.”
"If a bhikṣu, being not ill, lights a fire on open ground for the purpose of warming his body, or instructs another to light one, except at other times, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu hides another bhikṣu’s robe, bowl, sitting mat, or needle case—whether hiding it himself or instructing another to hide it—even if done merely in jest, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, having formally offered a robe to a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī, wears it without first asking the owner's permission, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣu obtains a new robe, he must apply one of three kinds of dyed discolored colors: blue, black, or madder-brown.
If a bhikṣu obtains a new robe and does not apply one of these three kinds of dyed discolored colors—blue, black, or madder-brown—but retains the new robe, it is a pāyattika.”
60. "If a bhikṣu intentionally takes the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu knows that water contains insects and drinks or uses it, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣu intentionally harasses another bhikṣu, even to the extent of causing him momentary displeasure, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense, conceals it, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣu is twenty years of age, he should be granted full ordination (*upasampadā*).
If a bhikṣu, knowing that one is not yet twenty years of age, grants him full ordination, this person does not obtain the precepts;
the other bhikṣus may also reprove him for his folly, and it is a *pāyattika* offense."
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that a dispute within the Saṃgha has arisen and has been settled according to the Dharma, should later reopen it, he commits a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that someone is a companion of thieves, should travel with them along the same path as far as a village, he commits a pāyattika offense."
"If a bhikṣu speaks thus:
'I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha that engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path,' that bhikṣu should admonish this bhikṣu, saying:"
"Venerable sir!
Do not speak such words; do not slander the Blessed One. It is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One, for the Blessed One does not speak thus.
By means of countless skillful methods, the Blessed One has declared that engaging in sexual misconduct is a dharma that obstructs the path."

When that bhikṣu thus admonishes him, if he persists and does not relinquish it, that bhikṣu should admonish him up to three times so that he may relinquish this matter; if he relinquishes it after being admonished up to three times, that is well.
"If he does not relinquish it, it is a pāyattika.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that such a person has not performed the formal act and has not relinquished such an evil view, should keep him as an associate, stay with him overnight, or perform the same *karmavācanā* with him, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu knows that a śrāmaṇera has spoken thus:
'I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha: engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path.'"
That bhikṣu should admonish this śrāmaṇera, saying:
"Do not speak such words; do not slander the World-Honored One. It is unwholesome to slander the World-Honored One, for the World-Honored One does not speak such things."
"Śrāmaṇera!
The World-Honored One, through countless skillful means, has declared that engaging in sexual desire is a dharma that obstructs the Path.
When that bhikṣu is thus admonished, if he persists and does not relinquish [his position], that bhikṣu should admonish him up to three times so that he may relinquish this matter.
Up to three admonitions, it is well if he relinquishes [the behavior].
If he does not relinquish it, that bhikṣu should say to this śrāmaṇera:
"From this day forward, you are no longer a disciple of the Buddha; you may not follow other bhikṣus as other śrāmaṇeras do, who are permitted to stay with a mahābhikṣu for two or three nights."
"You do not possess these qualities; depart! Be gone!
You need not remain here."
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that a śrāmaṇera has been thus expelled, should keep him as an attendant or share a lodging with him, it is a pāyattika.
Seventy: If a bhikṣu, when another bhikṣu is admonishing him in accordance with the Dharma, speaks thus:
'I will not study this precept; I shall wait until I have questioned those who are wise and uphold the Vinaya, and then I shall raise my objections.'"
[This constitutes] a *pāyattika*.
One who wishes to seek clarification should pose difficult questions [to resolve it].
"If a bhikṣu, at the time of reciting the precepts, speaks as follows:"
"Venerable Sir!
What is the use of these minor precepts?
When these precepts are recited, they cause people distress, shame, and doubt."
Because he has disparaged the precepts, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, at the time of reciting the precepts, speaks these words:
'Venerable sirs!'"
‘Only now do I know that this is the Dharma, this is the Sūtra of Precepts, which is recited every half-month within the Sūtra of Precepts.
If other bhikṣus know that this bhikṣu has sat through two or three recitations of the precepts, let alone more.
That bhikṣu is ignorant and lacks understanding; if he commits an offense, he should be dealt with according to the Dharma, and furthermore, his offense of ignorance shall be added.
"Venerable Sir!
You have gained no benefit and have acquired what is unwholesome."
"When you were reciting the precepts, you did not listen with a focused mind or pay close attention to the Dharma.
Because of this ignorance, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, after a formal ritual (*kamma*) has been performed together [with others], later speaks thus:"
"If a bhikṣu, out of favoritism toward those he is close to, gives monastic property to them,
it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣu,
when the Saṃgha is conducting formal business, rises and departs without having given his consent (chanda), it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, having given his consent (*chanda*), later reviles [the decision], it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that other bhikṣus are engaged in a quarrel, listens to their words and then reports them to those [involved], it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, strikes another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, strikes a bhikṣu with his hand, it is a pāyattika."
80. "If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, slanders another with a groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, it is a *pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣu enters the palace of a Kṣatriya king—anointed with water—while the king has not yet emerged and the treasures have not yet been stored away, and he passes over the threshold of the palace gate, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu, whether by himself or instructing another, takes hold of a jewel or an ornament made of jewels, except within a monastery or a lodging place, it is a pāyattika."

Whether in a monastery, or at a lodging place, if one takes hold of treasure or articles adorned with treasure, or causes another to take hold of them, it shall be taken by one who recognizes [the owner]; such is the cause and condition, and no other.
"If a bhikṣu enters a village at an improper time without having informed another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.

If a bhikṣu makes a rope bed or a wooden bed, the legs should be no higher than eight fingers of the Tathāgata; excluding the portion inserted into the mortise holes, if they exceed this length after being finished, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu takes cotton-wool and uses it to make a corded bed, a wooden bed, bedding, or a sitting cushion, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu makes a needle case from bone, ivory, or horn, once it is completed, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu makes a sitting mat (niṣīdana), he must make it according to the prescribed measurements. The measurement therein is:
two spans of the Buddha’s hand in length, one and a half spans in width; it may be increased by an additional half span in both length and width."
If one exceeds this, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu makes a cloth for covering sores, he should make it according to the prescribed measure.
The measure herein is: four spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and two spans in width."
If it exceeds these measurements, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika).
"If a bhikṣu makes a rain-bath robe, he should make it according to the prescribed measure.
The measure therein is: six spans of the Buddha’s hand in length, and two and a half spans in width."
If it exceeds [the prescribed measure] when completed, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu makes a robe equal in measure to the Buddha’s robe.
Herein, the measure is: ten spans (*vitasti*) of the Buddha in length and six spans in width; this is the measure of the Buddha’s robe."
If it exceeds [the limit] and is completed, it is a *pāyattika*.
(90) "Venerable sirs!
I have already recited the ninety *pāyattika* dharmas."
Now I ask the venerable ones:
Are you pure in this matter?
Thus it is asked three times: "Venerable ones!"
In this matter, we are pure, as indicated by our silence; thus shall this be upheld.
"Venerable sirs!
These four *pāṭidesanīya* dharmas are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra."

"If a bhikṣu, having entered a village and being free from illness, should receive food with his own hands from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative and eat it, that bhikṣu should confess to another bhikṣu, saying:
'Venerable sir!'"
"I have committed a censurable offense, which I ought not to have done; I now repent before the Venerable One.
This is called the procedure for repentance (*deśanā-vidhi*).
"If a bhikṣu is eating at the home of a layperson, and there is a bhikṣuṇī therein who directs, saying, 'Give soup to so-and-so' or 'Give rice to so-and-so'..."
The bhikṣus should speak to that bhikṣuṇī as follows:
"Sister, please stop for a moment;
wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating."
If not even a single bhikṣu says to that bhikṣuṇī:
"Sister, stop for a moment;
wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating."
That bhikṣu should confess his transgression to another bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir!
I have committed a censurable offense, which I ought not to have done; I now confess my transgression to you, Venerable sir."
This is called the method for repentance.
"There are families under training (*śaikṣa-kula*) for whom the Saṃgha has performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of declaring them as such.

If a bhikṣu, knowing such a family to be under training, accepts food with his own hands and eats it—without having previously received an invitation and while not being ill—that bhikṣu should confess his transgression to another bhikṣu, saying:"
"Venerable Sir!
I have committed a censurable offense, which ought not to have been done; I now repent before you, Venerable Sir.
This is called the procedure for repentance.
"If there is an *āraṇyaka* dwelling that is remote and in a place where there is apprehension or fear,
and if a bhikṣu resides in such an *āraṇyaka* location, he must not accept food outside the monastery grounds without first informing a donor."
If, within a monastery, a bhikṣu who is not ill receives food with his own hand and eats it, he should confess his transgression to another bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir!..."
"I have committed a censurable offense, which I ought not to have done; I now repent before the Venerable One.
This is called the procedure for repentance.
"Venerable Ones!..."
I have already explained the four *pāṭidesanīya* dharmas.
Now I ask the venerable ones:
Are you pure in this regard?
Thus it was said three times: "Venerable sirs!
In this matter we are pure, for we remain silent; thus shall this matter be held.
"Venerable sirs!"
These numerous rules of training are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra*:
"One should train to wear the inner robe neatly.
One should train to wear the three robes neatly."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with my robe tucked up over one shoulder.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with my robe tucked up over one shoulder.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with my robe wrapped around my neck.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with my robe wrapped around my neck.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not enter the house of a layperson with one's head covered.
One should train oneself: 'One must not sit in the house of a layperson with one's head covered.
One should train oneself: 'One must not enter the house of a layperson by leaping.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not skip rows to enter the house of a layperson and sit.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not squat while sitting in the house of a layperson.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with hands on my hips.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with hands on my hips.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson swaying the body.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not enter the house of a layperson swaying the body while seated.
One should train oneself: 'One must not enter the house of a layperson with dangling arms.
One should train oneself: 'One must not enter the house of a layperson and sit with dangling arms.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall enter the homes of laypeople with my body well-covered.
One should train oneself: 'I shall sit in the homes of laypeople with my body well-covered.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the homes of laypeople while looking here and there.'"
20. "One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson sitting while looking left and right.
One should train oneself: 'I shall enter the house of a layperson in silence.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall enter the house of a layperson in silence.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with frivolous laughter.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with frivolous laughter.'"
"One should train oneself to receive food with a composed mind.
One should train oneself to receive rice with a level bowl.
One should train oneself to receive soup with a level bowl."
"One should train oneself: 'One shall eat both soup and rice together.
One should train oneself: 'One shall eat in proper sequence.
(30) One should train oneself: 'One shall not pick at the center of the bowl while eating.'"
"One should train oneself: 'When not ill, one must not seek soup or rice for oneself.
One should train oneself: 'One must not cover the soup with rice in hopes of obtaining more.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not look into the bowl of one's neighbor and give rise to a mind of disdain.
One should train oneself: 'One should eat with the thought that the bowl is a tether.
One should train oneself: 'One must not take large mouthfuls of food.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not open one's mouth wide in anticipation of food.
One should train oneself: 'One must not speak with food in one's mouth.
One should train oneself: 'One must not take morsels of food and cast them into the mouth from a distance.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not let food fall [from the mouth].
One should train oneself: 'One must not eat with cheeks puffed out.

"Is there purity herein?
Thus it is asked three times:

"Venerable sirs! I have recited the introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra; I have recited the four pārājika rules; I have recited the thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣa rules; I have recited the two aniyata rules; I have recited the thirty naiḥsargika-pāyattika rules; I have recited the ninety pāyattika rules; I have recited the four pratideśanīya rules; I have recited the śaikṣa rules; and I have recited the seven adhikaraṇa-śamatha rules. This is the Prātimokṣa Sūtra spoken by the Buddha, which is recited every half-month from within the Prātimokṣa."
"If there are any other qualities of a Buddha, one should harmonize with them all and train accordingly.
"Patience is the supreme path; The Buddha has declared that non-action is foremost.
One who causes affliction to others while claiming to have left the home life Is not called a śramaṇa."
"This is the *Dharmapada* (Sīla-vagga) spoken by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin:
"Just as a person with clear vision Is able to avoid dangerous and evil paths,
So too, in this world, the wise person Is able to distance themselves from all evils."
"This is the Discourse on the Precepts spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Śikhin:
'Neither slandering nor envying, Always upholding the practice of the precepts,
Knowing moderation in food and drink, Always delighting in dwelling in seclusion.'"
"With a concentrated mind, delighting in diligence—this is called the teaching of all Buddhas.
This is the precept scripture spoken by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin.
"Just as a bee gathers from a flower, taking its nectar without damaging its color or fragrance;
so too, one should not interfere with the affairs of others, nor observe whether they have been done or left undone."
"Only observe your own conduct, whether it be right or wrong.
This is the precept scripture spoken by the Tathāgata Krakucchanda, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Do not be negligent in mind; you should diligently train in the noble Dharma.
Thus, free from sorrow, with a concentrated mind, you shall enter nirvana."
"This is the precept scripture spoken by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kanakamuni:
'Commit no evil whatsoever; Practice all that is good;
Completely purify your own mind— This is the teaching of the Buddhas.'"
"This is the Sutta on the Precepts spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa:
'Guard well your speech, Purify your own mind, Commit no evil with the body;
These three paths of action are pure. "
"One who is able to practice in this way follows the path of the Great Seer.
This is the *Pātimokkha* Sūtra spoken by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni for the community of monks free from worldly affairs over the course of twelve years.
From this point forward, I shall explain in detail.

Monks, those who delight in the Dharma, who delight in the life of a śramaṇa, who possess a sense of shame and a dread of blame, and who delight in training in the precepts, should train themselves therein.
“The wise person who can guard the precepts Shall obtain three kinds of happiness:
Renown and material gain, And upon death, rebirth in the heavens.
One should contemplate such states; The wise exert themselves to guard the precepts.”
With purity of precepts and wisdom, one attains the foremost path.
Just as the Buddhas of the past, those of the future,
and the World-Honored Ones of the present, are able to overcome all sorrow.
All together one should revere the precepts; this is the Dharma of all Buddhas.
If there are those who act for their own sake and desire to seek the Buddha-way, they should honor the True Dharma; this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
The Seven Buddhas, as World-Honored Ones, have extinguished all fetters and afflictions;
they have preached this Sūtra of the Seven Precepts, whereby all bonds are liberated,
they have entered Nirvāṇa, and all worldly play has been forever extinguished.
The Honored One, the Great Seer, has proclaimed the precepts praised by the noble and wise;
these are the practices of his disciples, leading them into the tranquility of nirvana.
When the World-Honored One was about to enter nirvana, he gave rise to great compassion.
Having assembled the community of bhikṣus, he gave them this instruction:
"Do not say that with my parinirvāṇa, those who practice purity will be without protection.
I now proclaim the Sūtra of Precepts and have also well-expounded the Vinaya."
Although I have entered parinirvāṇa, you should regard this sūtra as the World-Honored One.
As long as this sūtra remains in the world, the Buddha-dharma will flourish;
because it flourishes in this way, one shall attain entry into nirvāṇa.
If one does not uphold these precepts as they should be observed during the poṣadha, it is like the time when the sun sets: the world is plunged into total darkness.
One should guard and uphold these precepts, just as a yak cherishes its tail.
Gathered together in one place, seated as the Buddha has taught.
I have finished reciting the Prātimokṣa Sūtra; the Saṃgha’s Poṣadha ceremony is concluded.
Now that I have recited the Prātimokṣa Sūtra, may all the merits therein spoken be [attained].
